Revised assessment: The FOMC warns that COVID-19 will weigh on activity and pose downside risks, but its rapid move to the effective lower bound (0–0.25%), large-scale asset purchases ($500B Treasuries, $200B MBS), expanded repos, a lower discount rate, and coordinated dollar swap lines are well grounded in the credit view and bank-lending-channel literature (e.g., Oliner and Rudebusch, 1996a; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994). That work shows easing and liquidity support can stabilize funding markets, bolster bank balance sheets, and reduce the external finance premium, thereby mitigating real-side contractions. By reaffirming the symmetric 2% inflation objective and emphasizing expectations, the Fed aligns with inflation-forecast targeting ideas (Svensson) to keep long-run inflation expectations anchored despite falling market-based inflation compensation, helping limit time-inconsistency costs and adverse real-rate increases. Although liquidity-trap risks are present, the literature indicates non-rate tools and open-market operations in Treasuries/MBS can still influence longer-term yields and credit conditions. Net: near-term outlook remains negative due to the shock and weak investment/exports, but policy actions partially offset downside risks and support market functioning and credit flows.
